summary: This RFC defines an elliptic curve cryptography extension to the OpenPGP key format and specifies three curves widely supported in other standards, including some from NIST. It was replaced by RFC 9580.

eli5.summary: OpenPGP keeps secrets with math keys. This adds a newer kind of math that makes strong keys that are smaller.

questions: how to use elliptic curves in openpgp
how big is an ecdsa key
subtitle: Smaller, faster cryptographic keys for secure emails and messages.

tldr.problem: OpenPGP supported RSA and DSA for signing and key exchange, but these algorithms require very large keys to achieve modern security levels, consuming more bandwidth and processing power.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds support for Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) to OpenPGP, specifying three standardized NIST curves (P-256, P-384, P-521) and defining how ECDSA signs messages and ECDH exchanges keys.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use smaller, faster ECC keys with equivalent security to much larger RSA keys, improving performance and compatibility with Suite-B government cryptographic standards.

today: RFC 6637 was replaced by RFC 9580, which updates the ECC extension to OpenPGP. The core concept remains in use: ECC has become standard in modern OpenPGP implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The OpenPGP protocol [RFC4880] has traditionally relied on RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) and DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) for public key operations. This RFC extends OpenPGP to support Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), offering a more efficient alternative that achieves the same security with much smaller keys.

An ECDSA key with 256 bits provides equivalent security to an RSA key with 3072 bits. This means ECC keys are faster to generate, smaller to transmit, and quicker to use in cryptographic operations. The RFC standardizes support for ECC in OpenPGP while maintaining backward compatibility with existing RSA and DSA implementations.
sections.eli5: Math keys come in many flavors. This adds a new flavor called ECC that works with much smaller numbers but is just as secure.

sections.title: The Three Standard Curves
sections.content:
The RFC specifies three elliptic curves, all defined by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and published in FIPS 186-3. These are Curve P-256 (also called NIST P-256), Curve P-384, and Curve P-521. All three are prime field curves, meaning they perform arithmetic modulo a large prime number.

The three curves offer different security levels. P-256 provides 128-bit security and should be the minimum any compliant OpenPGP implementation supports; P-384 offers 192-bit security; and P-521 provides 256-bit security. The number in the curve name refers roughly to the key size in bits. Each curve is identified by an Object Identifier (OID) encoded as a sequence of bytes in the key format.
sections.eli5: The RFC picks three standard curves, like three sizes of keys: small (P-256), medium (P-384), and large (P-521), so people can pick the strength they need.

sections.title: Signature and Key Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two algorithms. ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) is used for signing documents and creating digital signatures, and ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) is used to establish a shared secret between two parties who can then encrypt a message together.

ECDSA works by signing a hash of the message with the signer's private key, and anyone with the public key can verify the signature. ECDH allows Alice and Bob to each generate ephemeral key pairs and exchange their public keys, then both compute the same shared secret without ever sending the secret itself. OpenPGP implementations MUST support both ECDSA and ECDH.
sections.eli5: ECDSA signs messages like a handwritten signature. ECDH is a secret handshake where two people both end up knowing the same secret without saying it out loud.

sections.title: ECDH and Key Wrapping
sections.content:
The ECDH process in OpenPGP is more complex than simple key exchange. When one person wants to send an encrypted message to another, the sender generates an ephemeral ECDH key pair for that message only. Both parties compute a shared secret using ECDH; the sender then passes this shared secret through a Key Derivation Function (KDF) to produce a symmetric encryption key.

The symmetric key is used to wrap (encrypt) the message's session key using AES key wrap (from RFC 3394). This wrapped session key is then sent along with an MPI (multiprecision integer) containing the ephemeral public key. The recipient can recover the shared secret using their private key, derive the same symmetric key, unwrap the session key, and decrypt the message. The RFC requires that a Modification Detection Code (MDC) be used whenever ECDH is employed.
sections.eli5: ECDH in OpenPGP is like a mailbox system: both people compute the same combination lock, use it to lock a smaller key inside, and mail the locked box. The recipient uses their copy of the combination to open the box and get the key.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security Levels
sections.content:
The RFC defines two compatibility profiles. The OpenPGP ECC Profile requires all implementations to support P-256, optionally support P-384, and recommend P-521. Implementations must support SHA-256 for hashing and should support the stronger SHA-384 and SHA-512. For encryption, AES-128 is required; AES-256 is recommended.

The Suite-B Profile aligns OpenPGP with the NSA Suite-B government cryptographic standards. It defines two security levels: 128-bit security uses P-256 with AES-128 and SHA-256, and 192-bit security uses P-384 with AES-256 and SHA-384. A table in the RFC maps each curve to its corresponding hash and symmetric encryption algorithms to maintain balanced cryptographic strength throughout the system.
sections.eli5: Different organizations have different rules about which curves and hash functions to use together. The RFC defines two standard recipes so everyone knows what works well together.
